source: 26 real auction threads from truedungeon.com, one per recorded auction, spanning 21 of the 33 forum auctioneers. Verbatim pages, gzipped, nothing trimmed — for the same reason fixtures/auction-open gives: the failures this guards against are matches found in the wrong place on the page, and a trimmed page cannot show one.
pagination: Kunena serves 12 posts to a page. Every page of every thread is here, because two of the assistant's outputs — the close-date evidence and the withheld candidates — live in later posts, not in the results post. `topic-N.html.gz` is page 1 and `topic-N-startM.html.gz` is the page beginning at post M.
sharedWithPhase4: Page 1 of 248428, 248693, 252093, 255503, 258020, 259475 and 259798 is NOT duplicated here — it already lives in fixtures/auction-open, which Phase 4 fetched from the same markup to read open dates. The test resolves page 1 from either directory. Copying them would leave two versions of one page in the repo, free to disagree after a re-fetch.

expect.why: The corpus totals, pinned so a regression reads as a number. `reproduces` is the quantity-weighted mode against prices.csv; `min` and `max` are what Trent's rule would have proposed from the same distributions, and the gap between them is the evidence that a thread wants a mode and a Trent file wants a pair. `closeBracketHits` is 7 of the 15 threads that yield a bracket at all, which is why the close date is reported as evidence and never proposed.

threads.why: TWO grammars in one post: a `Item | # | High Bidder | Current Bid` tab table for the premium items, and a headerless `qty | buyer | price` table for the trade goods beneath it. The header does not fit the second, so the reader falls back to reading it positionally — held to the first header those forty lines read as nothing at all. Also the plan's known disagreement: the thread says the Patron Pin went for $2.00 and the sheet records $1.25.

The results are a real HTML `<table>`, not tab-separated text — the only one in the corpus. Without a separator between cells the row arrives as `2019 Orb of Dragonkind1+$5.00$605maelios`. Also a thread whose post still says `Current Bids`, so its Patron Pin is $100.25 against a recorded $100.
The lot-RANGE grammar: `#1-3 : Lich - $100` is three tokens, not one. Reproduces every item it matches.
`1 $5.00 - Osiris` under an item heading ending in a colon — the count with no `x`, which means the price is each.

`Item (Qty) - $Price Buyer`, and `PYP 1 - $115.00 Moon` where the number is a lot number in the name. Carries the corpus's one true midpoint: Aragonite went 5 @ $16 and 5 @ $17 and is recorded as $16.50.

THE DROP CASE and THE AMBIGUITY CASE. `NON-8K STUFF` heads twenty of his own tokens that 20222 records nowhere at all — not in prices, not in contextItems. And nine lots are marked `ONYX or PYP`, which the sheet resolved BOTH ways: all nine are onyx.csv rows and their $110 is what prices.csv records as Ultra Rare. Also `x35 @ $12.25` — thirty-five bars at $12.25 each, the opposite of Flik's `10x $25`, and the `@` is the only thing that says so. The 21st Onyx row is the `Common, Uncommon, Rare Sets` line the sheet omitted in 2022 and has included since.

Matt Soto's grammar in another hand, with pseudonymous buyers (`16 @ $7.50 - Bidder #4`). Reproduces everything it matches — and its close-date bracket is 24 days early, the worst miss in the corpus and the reason that output is evidence rather than a proposal.

RESULTS IN POST #2, and NO DOLLAR SIGN ANYWHERE: `Orion's Belt (1) 150 Chronos`. A `$`-anchored parser reads this thread as empty. Its two Onyx rows — `Onyx Lucky Kilt` and `Onyx Death Knight Mail`, tokens he added from his own collection — are recorded NOWHERE: 202231 has no onyx.csv rows and no contextItems rows at all. Surfacing them is the assistant working, not failing, so the expected count here is what the thread says rather than what the sheet holds.
`Wish Ring (1) - $175.00 Abert` — the most common forum grammar there is, shared with Ralykam and with Wade S from 2025 on.

THE SECTION-END CASE. `ONYX ITEMS` is followed by `TRADE GOODS`, and without a rule that closes a section the Onyx heading runs to the bottom of the post: 33 Onyx rows proposed against 21 recorded, and eleven trade goods lost from the price spine. Its one tie, the Guild Button at 2 @ $1 against 2 @ $1.25, is recorded HIGH.
The plan's own worked example for the close-date bracket, and it lands: Feb 23-27 against a recorded Feb 25.
NO RESULTS ANYWHERE IN THE THREAD. The auction closed and shipped and the numbers were never posted. One of two threads that must produce nothing without pretending otherwise.
RESULTS IN POST #2, buyer-first (`- Anton (1) $780`), and the lot size written into the BUYER field: `- 10x Chips = Calnasse (4) $33` is four lots of ten at $3.30 a token.
`(3) Lanfear====@ $105 each`. Two of its three misses are ties that resolved high.
The second thread with no posted results — the bids lived in a Google Sheet linked from post #1.
`10x 2025 Treasure Chips (5) - $35.00 Oghma` — the lot size in the NAME rather than on the line, which is `parseQuantity`'s rule and is shared with Trent unchanged.
The same auctioneer as 20181 seven years later, writing a completely different grammar. Whatever a parser learns from an auctioneer's old thread, it cannot assume about the new one.
PRICE LAST, BUYER IN THE MIDDLE: `Mark of the 1st Tenet (1) - Gortash $85`. Identical in shape to Beertram's line and reversed in meaning, so rule order is what tells them apart.

THE `Buy It Out` TRAP. The table is headed `item name | Buy It Out | Bid | Bidder/Buyer Name`: the money-formatted column is a buy-it-now price, identical down every row of an item, and the winning bid is the bare column beside it. Reading the formatting scores 6; reading the header scores 14. Its unresolved lines are exactly the five grunnel and augment rows contextItems carries for this auction.

threads.onyxNote: 21, not the 20 measured before the item-price-dash-buyer grammar existed. `Onyx Greaves of Diffusion - $65 - Allen` puts a DASH before the buyer where the rest of this post puts a space, so it was the one Onyx line no grammar read. onyx.csv records 21 rows for this auction, so 21 is the reconciling number and the old 20 was encoding the miss.
threads.why: The plan's withheld example, verbatim: "For this auction I am keeping the 9-10 random URs, 2 OE and 2 EB out." Quantities as a RANGE, which is why withheld candidates are quoted for a human rather than parsed into a row.

THE `Nx` CASE, both ways in one post. Under `Alchemist's Ink (33)`, `10x $25` is ten tokens for $25 — $2.50 each. Under `Aragonite (12 - individual)`, `9x $11` is nine tokens at $11 each. Only the heading's `individual` tells them apart, and getting it wrong is a factor of ten either way. Also `+2 Branding Mace // $42 - Samantha` under an `Onyx URs (16)` heading, where the heading is the ONLY thing marking sixteen chase tokens as Onyx — and `Standard Onyx 8k Items`, a heading that must NOT be read as one.

The file path's auctioneer. He posts no per-item results at all — the thread links a tracking spreadsheet — which is exactly why part one exists. Present so the two halves of Phase 5 are visibly complementary rather than overlapping.

threads.withheldQuote: only keeping the eight Rings of the First Circle
threads.why: THE REPOSTED-SNAPSHOT CASE, and the reason post #1 wins. He reposts the whole table as a bid update: 80 of its 165 posts carry a near-complete copy and the BIGGEST copy is a mid-auction snapshot whose prices are lower. "The post with the most lots" picks that one and reproduces nothing; post #1, edited in place after the close, reproduces all fifteen. Its withheld sentence appears 71 times and is 4 distinct sentences, which is why candidates are deduped — and the right one, `Ring of the 1st Circle` × 8, is exactly what contextItems records. Also `Tabor's onyx dagger #3`, a physical prop that must NOT be routed to onyx.csv just for containing the word.
The auction part one imports from a file. No per-item results in the thread, but its close-date bracket lands exactly on the recorded date — the plan's second worked example.

THE CONDENSED-BAG CASE. A Condensed order sells a bag of 120 random Rares and a bag of 240 random Uncommons, which no Super or Ultra Condensed auction has. This auctioneer writes them `8 x 120 Random Rare bag`, and that leading `8 x ` is read by the shared quantity rule as a lot of 8 — so the $100 bag divides to $12.50 unless a bag is exempted. Its two recorded bag prices are reproduced exactly, which is what pins both halves of the fix. itemsMatched is 0 because this auctioneer's other line grammars are not supported; the bags are what this fixture is here for.

A Condensed auction MISSING its bag rows — one of three found by the new check. Its `TOKEN BAGS` section sells `Bag of 120x Rare Tokens` and `Bag of 240x Uncommon Tokens`, and the Rare Bag is a genuine 4-4 tie ($70 and $65), so it exercises the tie flag on a proposal for data the sheet does not yet hold.
